item.title: [AHA Hist 2025] When Big Oil Managed Love: The Prize-Winning History of Refineries That Tried to Run Caribbean Family Life
item.body:
> Historian Chelsea Schields' award-winning book *Offshore Attachments* shows how the giant oil refineries on Curaçao and Aruba didn't just process crude — they reached deep into people's private lives, shaping marriage, sex work, and family planning to keep the oil flowing.

## What Was Presented

At the American Historical Association's 138th annual meeting, held in New York in January 2025, Chelsea Schields, associate professor of history at the University of California, Irvine, received the AHA Prize in European International History Since 1895 for her book *Offshore Attachments: Oil and Intimacy in the Caribbean* (University of California Press, 2023).

The book tells a story most of us have never heard. By the mid-twentieth century, two small Dutch Caribbean islands — Curaçao and Aruba — hosted some of the largest oil refineries in the world. Shell ran a massive facility on Curaçao, and Standard Oil operated another on Aruba. These plants refined crude shipped in from Venezuela and helped fuel the Allied war effort in World War II.

Schields' central argument is that this industrial boom was never just about pipes and tankers. To staff the refineries, companies recruited tens of thousands of migrant workers from across the Caribbean, often housing them in segregated camps divided by nationality. And to manage this largely male workforce, corporations and colonial authorities began managing intimacy itself. On Curaçao, authorities sanctioned a regulated brothel, Campo Alegre, staffed by women recruited from Colombia and the Dominican Republic on short-term contracts — a cheaper option, officials reasoned, than paying wages high enough for workers to bring their families. Company magazines celebrated employee weddings and preached lessons about responsible fatherhood. Later, when automation slashed jobs, officials promoted birth-control campaigns aimed largely at Afro-Curaçaoan women, blaming working-class families' size for unemployment rather than the industry's own decisions.

Crucially, Caribbean people were not passive in this story. In 1951, roughly three thousand Aruban housewives protested plans for a brothel on their island — and won. Schields traces how islanders embraced, negotiated, and resisted these intrusions, and follows the story onward as Caribbean migrants moved to the Netherlands after the refineries declined in the 1970s and 1980s.

The AHA's prize citation called the book "groundbreaking," noting that Schields used sources in five languages to show how sex and race organized oil production and shaped a transnational labor market. The book also collected several other major honors, including the AHA's Joan Kelly Memorial Prize.

## Why It Matters

We usually tell the history of oil through geopolitics: embargoes, pipelines, price shocks. Schields flips the camera around and shows the human infrastructure underneath — the bedrooms, kitchens, and family arguments that the energy economy quietly depended on.

That shift matters in at least three ways. First, it redraws the map. Histories of "European international history" typically center on London, Paris, or Berlin; this book shows that decisions made in Caribbean oil towns shaped Europe's wealth and its postwar migration, making two small islands central to a global story.

Second, it speaks to the present. Debates about energy transition often focus on technology and markets, but Schields reminds us that energy systems restructure ordinary life — who moves where for work, who raises children and under what pressure, whose bodies bear the costs. Any future energy shift will have its own intimate consequences.

Third, it's a case study in corporate power. The book documents how far companies once went beyond the factory gate — into sex, reproduction, and family — when profit seemed to require it. That history offers a sobering benchmark for thinking about employer influence over private life today.

## An Easy Way to Understand It

Think of a "company town" — a place where one employer owns the housing, the store, and effectively the whole local economy. Now imagine the company doesn't stop at your paycheck and your rent. It decides whether your spouse can join you on the island, prints your wedding announcement in its magazine as a model of good behavior, arranges regulated sex work so it can avoid paying family wages, and — when it needs fewer workers — sponsors campaigns nudging your community to have fewer children. That is what Schields means by "offshoring" intimacy: just as firms move factories offshore to escape inconvenient regulations, oil companies and officials moved the private side of labor into legal gray zones where the usual rules about sex and family could be bent to fit the balance sheet.

## In Three Lines

1. Chelsea Schields won the AHA Prize in European International History Since 1895, conferred at the AHA annual meeting in January 2025, for *Offshore Attachments: Oil and Intimacy in the Caribbean*.
2. The book shows how oil companies and colonial authorities on Curaçao and Aruba managed workers' intimate lives — from regulated sex work to birth-control campaigns — to maximize refinery profits.
3. It reframes energy history as a story about people and relationships, showing that Caribbean islanders both shaped and resisted the oil economy that ran through their homes.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Refinery**: An industrial plant that turns crude oil into usable products like gasoline; Curaçao and Aruba hosted some of the world's largest in the mid-1900s.
- **Offshoring**: Moving business activity to another jurisdiction to cut costs or avoid regulation — a concept Schields extends to how companies handled workers' private lives.
- **History of intimacy**: A field of history that studies private life — sex, marriage, reproduction, kinship — as a force shaping politics and economics.
- **Dutch Caribbean**: Caribbean islands, including Curaçao and Aruba, that were part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands during the twentieth-century oil boom.
- **AHA Prize in European International History Since 1895**: An American Historical Association book award for outstanding work on Europe's role in international history after 1895.
